sections.title: Introduction
sections.text:
Welcome. Today's story is so famous that its title has become an everyday phrase. Whenever someone small takes on someone big, people call it a “David and Goliath” match-up. But the real story, found in First Samuel chapters sixteen and seventeen, is not mainly about an underdog. It's about a young man who trusted God, and about a God who looks at the heart.

As you listen, think about the “giants” in your own life — the problems that seem too big to face. What would it look like to face them the way David did?

sections.title: The Story, Part 1
sections.text:
Israel's first king, Saul, had disobeyed God, and God had rejected him as king. So the Lord sent the prophet Samuel to Bethlehem, to the house of a man named Jesse, to anoint one of Jesse's sons as the next king.

Jesse's sons came before Samuel one by one. The first was Eliab — tall and impressive. Samuel thought, surely this is the one. But God said something we all need to hear. First Samuel chapter sixteen, verse seven: “Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.”

Seven of Jesse's sons passed by, and God chose none of them. Samuel asked, “Are here all thy children?” Jesse said there was one more, the youngest, out keeping the sheep. No one had even thought to invite him. They sent for David, and when he came, the Lord said, “Arise, anoint him: for this is he.” Samuel poured oil on David's head, and the Spirit of the Lord came upon David from that day forward.

Some time later, the Philistines gathered their armies against Israel. The two armies faced each other on two mountains with a valley in between. And every morning and every evening, a champion came out from the Philistine camp. His name was Goliath, of Gath. He stood over nine feet tall. He wore a bronze helmet and a coat of armor that weighed about a hundred and twenty-five pounds, and the head of his spear alone weighed about fifteen pounds. He shouted across the valley, choose a man and let him come fight me. If he wins, we will be your servants. If I win, you will be ours. For forty days he defied Israel, and King Saul and all his soldiers were dismayed and greatly afraid.

sections.title: The Story, Part 2
sections.text:
David's three oldest brothers were in Saul's army. One day Jesse sent David with food for them. As David arrived, Goliath came out and shouted his challenge, and David watched the soldiers of Israel run away in fear. David couldn't believe it. He asked, “who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?”

His oldest brother Eliab was angry and accused David of pride. But David kept asking, and his words reached King Saul. David told the king, let no one lose heart. I will go and fight this Philistine. Saul said, you are only a youth, and he has been a warrior since his youth.

David explained that while keeping his father's sheep, a lion and a bear had come and taken a lamb, and he had gone after them and rescued the lamb and killed them both. Then he said, in First Samuel chapter seventeen, verse thirty-seven: “The LORD that delivered me out of the paw of the lion, and out of the paw of the bear, he will deliver me out of the hand of this Philistine.” Saul said, “Go, and the LORD be with thee.”

Saul dressed David in his own armor and gave him his sword. But David had never tested them, and he could hardly walk. So he took them off. He took his staff, chose five smooth stones out of the brook, put them in his shepherd's bag, and went out with his sling in his hand.

When Goliath saw David, he despised him because he was only a youth, and he cursed David by his gods. Then David answered with some of the boldest words in Scripture. First Samuel chapter seventeen, verse forty-five: “Thou comest to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a shield: but I come to thee in the name of the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom thou hast defied.” And he added, so that all the earth may know there is a God in Israel, “for the battle is the LORD's.”

As Goliath came closer, David ran toward him. He put his hand in his bag, took out a stone, and slung it. The stone struck the Philistine in the forehead, and Goliath fell on his face to the earth. When the Philistines saw that their champion was dead, they fled, and Israel won a great victory that day.

sections.title: The Lesson
sections.text:
What can we learn from David?

First, God looks at the heart. People overlooked David; even his own father didn't think to call him in from the field. But God saw a heart that loved and trusted Him. You may feel overlooked, but God sees you.

Second, faithfulness in small things prepares us for big things. David learned to trust God while protecting sheep, far from any crowd. Those quiet battles with the lion and the bear prepared him for the giant. The ordinary, unseen places where you serve today matter to God.

Third, courage comes from remembering what God has already done. David didn't say, I'm strong enough. He said, God delivered me before, and He will deliver me again. When you face a giant, remember how God has helped you in the past.

And finally, the battle is the Lord's. David didn't win because of his skill with a sling. He won because he went out in the name of the Lord. Our biggest problems — sickness, money troubles, broken relationships, fear — are not bigger than our God.

sections.title: Prayer and Reflection
sections.text:
Name the giant you are facing right now. Then name one way God has helped you before. Hold those two things side by side.

Let's pray. Lord of hosts, thank You that You look at the heart. Thank You for every time You have helped me in the past. Give me courage to face the giants in my life, not in my own strength, but in Your name. The battle is Yours. In Jesus' name, Amen.

Thank you for listening. Next time, we'll hear about a prophet who tried to run away from God: Jonah.
